title: Work packages, estimates, schedule and budget
blurb: Describe the planning steps after the products are defined: organizing work packages, estimating, scheduling, analysing risks, budgeting and documenting the plan.
question: A project manager has defined the products and grouped the delivery activities into work packages. Which planning steps follow before the plan can be documented?

teach.h: From products to a finished plan
teach.body: Once the products are defined and analysed, the planning technique continues: organizing work packages, preparing estimates, preparing the schedule and preparing the budget, then documenting the plan. Analysing risks runs alongside all of these. The same technique is repeated for the project plan, stage plans and team plans. Plain English: having decided what to make, work out who does which bundle of work, how long and how much, and what could go wrong.

teach.caption: Analysing risks runs alongside every step: a plan stays in draft until its risks have been addressed.

teach.body: When the delivery approach is decided, the delivery activities for each product are identified and grouped into work packages. The project manager makes sure there is no overlap in scope between any two work packages and no gaps. The project plan identifies the proposed work packages, which form the top level of the project's work breakdown structure; each work package is later handed to a team manager through a work package description.

teach.caption: Work packages form the top level of the WBS. Each covers a distinct set of products, so nothing is done twice and nothing is missed.

head: Technique
In short
rows: Overall figure split across the parts
Estimate each part, then add up
Apply known rates to measured units
For example Delphi or planning poker
teach.caption: Project managers and team managers always plan using estimates. Lessons from past projects improve them.

teach.body: A schedule captures the sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks. Every work package for a stage must appear in that stage's schedule. Team managers prepare the schedules for their work packages. Throughout, the plan is analysed for risks: new threats and opportunities are identified, and the plan is not finalized until they are addressed.

teach.caption: All three work packages appear in the stage schedule, with their sequence and dependencies.
The budget covers the cost of the activities, plus any risk budget, change budget and cost tolerances.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Harlow Fields Health Centre
teach.body: Project manager Nadia Hussain is preparing the stage plan for a clinic refurbishment at Harlow Fields Health Centre. She groups the work into three work packages, asks each team manager for bottom-up estimates and their schedules, and checks the result against similar past refits. She adds a risk budget for asbestos surveys and a small change budget. Finally she documents the plan: dependencies, tolerances, controls, budgets, risks and assumptions, ready for board approval.

teach.text: Risk budget and change budget are not the same. A risk budget funds the responses to risks; a change budget funds approved changes to what is being delivered. Both are optional parts of a plan's budget, and neither is the same as cost tolerance.

items: After defining products: organize work packages, estimate, schedule, budget, document; analyse risks alongside.
Work packages: no overlap, no gaps; the project plan's proposed work packages are the top level of the WBS.
Estimating techniques include top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics and expert consensus (Delphi, planning poker).
Schedule: sequence, interrelationships and duration; all of a stage's work packages are in its schedule.
Budget: activity costs plus optional risk and change budgets and cost tolerances.

summary: You can now describe the planning steps that follow product analysis: organizing work packages, estimating, scheduling, analysing risks, budgeting and documenting the plan. You can also tell a risk budget from a change budget and name common estimating techniques.

A.q: In which planning step are delivery activities grouped so that there is no overlap and no gap between them?
A.why: Organizing work packages groups the delivery activities, with no overlap in scope between any two work packages (7.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: Scheduling sequences the work packages and tasks once they exist.
whyNot.2: Budgeting costs the work and adds any risk and change budgets.
whyNot.3: Documenting the plan writes up the narrative once the other steps are done.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks are captured in a [?].
A.why: A schedule captures the sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and tasks (7.3.1.4).

whyNot.1: The budget holds costs, not sequence and duration.
whyNot.2: The product register lists products and their status.
whyNot.3: A work package description passes one package to a team manager; it is not the stage-wide sequence.

A.q: Which is an estimating technique based on reaching expert consensus?
A.why: Expert consensus techniques such as Delphi or planning poker are among the estimating techniques (7.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: MoSCoW is a prioritization technique, not an estimating technique.
whyNot.1: Quality review checks a product against its quality specifications.
whyNot.2: Escalating forecast breaches of tolerance is how the progress practice applies manage by exception; it does not produce estimates.

B.q:
Which two statements about the budget in a plan are correct?
1. A risk budget funds the responses to risks.
2. A change budget funds approved changes.
3. A risk budget funds approved requests for change.
4. A change budget is required in every plan.
B.why: A risk budget funds risk responses and a change budget funds approved changes; both are optional (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: approved changes are funded by the change budget.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: risk and change budgets are optional parts of a plan's budget.
whyNot.2: Both are false: risk budgets do not fund changes, and change budgets are optional.

B.q: Who prepares the schedule for each work package?
B.why: The team manager prepares schedules for each work package (tab 7.1).

whyNot.0: The project manager prepares the project and stage plans and the work package descriptions.
whyNot.2: Project support assists with compiling plans and maintains planning tools.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and keeps plans consistent with the supplier view.

B.q: When are risks analysed in the planning technique?
options: After the plan is approved, in the first highlight report
Before the products are defined, so they shape the PBS
Alongside the other steps, before the plan is finalized
At the end of the stage, when the plan is reviewed
B.why: Analysing risks runs alongside the other planning steps; a plan stays in draft until its risks are addressed (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: Waiting until after approval means the board approves a plan whose risks are unknown.
whyNot.1: Risk analysis accompanies the planning steps rather than replacing product definition as the start.
whyNot.3: End-of-stage review is too late for the plan's own risks to shape it.

C.q: Which statement about work packages in the project plan is correct?
options: It lists each team's daily tasks for the project
It replaces the need for work package descriptions
Its work packages are agreed by team managers in SU
It identifies proposed work packages, the top of the WBS
C.why: The project plan identifies the proposed work packages, which typically form the top level of the work breakdown structure (7.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Daily tasks are far too detailed for the high-level project plan; schedules and team plans hold them.
whyNot.1: Work package descriptions are still used to pass responsibility for each package formally.
whyNot.2: The project plan is created in IP, and team managers accept work packages in MP.

C.q: All work packages for a stage must appear in which document, and which step of the technique produces it?
options: The stage schedule; preparing the schedule
The product breakdown structure; defining products
The project brief; organizing work packages
C.why: All work packages for a stage must be included in the schedule for that stage, produced in the 'preparing the schedule' step (7.3.1.4).

whyNot.1: The PBS lists products, not work packages, and comes from defining and analysing products.
whyNot.2: The project brief is a starting-up product and does not hold the stage's work packages.
whyNot.3: The quality register records quality activities, not work packages.

C.q: Which is NOT part of preparing a plan's budget?
options: The cost of the planned activities
A risk budget for risk responses
A benefits tolerance for the stage
A change budget for approved changes
C.why: A plan's budget covers activity costs, any risk budget and change budget, and cost tolerances (7.3.1). Benefits tolerance is a separate tolerance area, not part of the budget.

whyNot.0: Activity costs are the core of the budget.
whyNot.1: A risk budget is an optional part of the budget.
whyNot.3: A change budget is an optional part of the budget.

reteach.title: Planning a house move
reteach.question: Once you know what is moving, how do you turn that into a workable plan?

blocks.body: You split the move into bundles: packing, removal van, utilities (work packages, no overlaps). You estimate each, perhaps from last time (comparative). You put them in order on a calendar (schedule). You add a small fund for breakages (risk budget) and for any extra items you decide to take (change budget). Then you write it down so everyone knows the plan.

blocks.text: Breakages fund = risk budget. Extra items you choose to take = change budget. Keep them apart.

explain.body: Delivery activities are grouped into work packages once the delivery approach is decided, with no overlap and no gaps between them.

test.q: What should the project manager check when organizing work packages?
options: That every work package has its own stage
That no two work packages overlap in scope
That each work package has a benefits tolerance
That team managers write the project plan
test.why: The project manager makes sure there is no overlap in the scope of any two work packages, and no gaps (7.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: A stage normally contains several work packages.
whyNot.2: Work package tolerances cover scope, cost and time, not benefits.
whyNot.3: The project manager prepares the project plan.

explain.body: Project managers and team managers always plan using estimates, drawing on techniques such as top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics and expert consensus.

test.q: A team manager estimates each task in a work package and adds them up. Which technique is this?
test.why: Estimating each part and adding them up is bottom-up estimating (7.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Top-down starts with an overall figure and splits it across the parts.
whyNot.1: Comparative estimating uses similar past work as the reference.
whyNot.3: Parametric estimating applies known rates to measured units.

explain.body: The schedule sets the order, links and duration of work packages and tasks. Team managers prepare schedules for their work packages.

options: The products of the plan as a hierarchy
The cost of each activity and the risk budget
The tolerances agreed for each work package
The sequence, links and duration of work
test.why: A schedule captures the sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and tasks (7.3.1.4).

whyNot.0: A hierarchy of products is the product breakdown structure.
whyNot.1: Costs and the risk budget belong to the budget step.
whyNot.2: Work package tolerances are recorded in the work package description.

explain.body: The last step writes the narrative around the schedule and budget: dependencies, tolerances, controls, budgets, risks and assumptions.

test.q: Which is the final step of the PRINCE2 planning technique?
test.why: Documenting the plan is the final step, adding the narrative of dependencies, tolerances, controls, budgets, risks and assumptions (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: Preparing the budget comes just before documenting the plan.
whyNot.2: Analysing risks runs alongside the other steps rather than coming last.
whyNot.3: The schedule is prepared before the budget and documentation.
